Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is building "Vibe Voyager" — an interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering practices. It will be hosted at [REDACTED_DOMAIN] on Vercel (free tier). The user is giving a lecture in ~1 week (from 2026-03-07) and wants a full game experience (not just a course with game skin). The game should take a beginner in software engineering to an "agentic developer / AI engineer" capable of utilizing world-class practices. The user explicitly wants to use agent teams with Claude Code (superpowers + compound engineering plugins) to build at scale — they've coded 50k+ lines in two days before. They also want a "How This Was Built" meta section documenting the entire process.

   - **Motion** package (formerly Framer Motion) — import from `motion/react`, NOT `framer-motion`
   - **Tailwind CSS v4** — CSS-first config with `@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme` directive, no tailwind.config.js
   - **Howler.js** for audio (ambient loops + SFX sprites, 7kb gzipped)
   - **HTML5 Canvas** for star map and mini-games
   - **localStorage** for all game state (no backend, no database, no auth)
   - **Vercel free tier** hosting with custom domain
   - **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) — agent-to-tool communication, 97M monthly downloads, 1.0 spec targeting June 2026
   - **A2A** (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) — Google's agent interoperability protocol, 150+ enterprise partners, Linux Foundation
   - **Karpathy's evolution:** "vibe coding" (Feb 2025) → "agentic engineering" (Feb 2026) — this IS the game's narrative arc
   - **Agent SDKs:** Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK (evolved from Swarm), Google ADK
   - **AGENTS.md** — cross-tool standard for configuring AI agents, 60k+ projects, Linux Foundation
   - **AI Code Quality 2026 data:** 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS, 4x more code cloning in AI-generated code
   - **Color System:** Void (#0a0f1a), Nebula Blue (#4a6fa5), Signal Green (#6b9e78), Core Terracotta (#c17147), Starlight (#e8e0d4), Glass (rgba(255,255,255,0.05))
   - **Typography:** Space Grotesk (display), Inter (body), JetBrains Mono (code)
   - **4 Player Stats:** Vibe, Architecture, Protocol, Command (each 1-10)
   - **4 Ranks:** Cadet (4-10) → Navigator (11-20) → Commander (21-30) → Admiral (31-40)
   - **5 Crew Members:** ARIA (narrator), Scout (Perceive), Archie (Plan), Exec (Act), Mirror (Reflect)
   - **6 Challenge Types:** Prompt Duel, Architect, Connect, Debug, Command, Dialogue

3. Files and Code Sections:

Contains all 10 sections: audience, narrative, tech stack, project structure, game systems, planet content map, Academy sections, UX flow, content gaps, build approach. Was being actively updated with gap analysis findings when summary was requested. Academy sections were being renumbered after inserting new "Agent SDKs & Protocols" section.

I know you're mostly relying on the content i provided via gemini research and notebookLM (which you should move in its own folder) but would you also like to conduct your own research and maybe find any gaps that should be covered but aren't being covered from a content standpoint as well?"

# Vibe Voyager — Design Document

> An interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering practices. From beginner to agentic developer.

**URL:** [REDACTED_DOMAIN]
**Hosting:** Vercel (free tier)
**Target:** Lecture demo + standalone learning platform
**Deadline:** ~2026-03-14

---

## 1. Audience

Mixed levels with multiple entry points:
- Software engineering students who code but haven't used AI tools
- Working developers adopting agentic workflows
- Beginners exploring AI-assisted development
- The Academy section is accessible without playing the game (direct access for anyone)

## 2. Narrative Arc

**Key narrative thread:** The game mirrors Karpathy's own evolution — he coined "vibe coding" (Feb 2025), then declared it "passé" and introduced **"agentic engineering"** (Feb 2026). The player lives this arc.

### Act 1 — "The Solo Pilot" (Beginner) — Vibe Coding
Player wakes as a rookie developer in a single-person ship. Learns to fly by talking to ship AI (vibe coding). Fast but fragile — tech debt accumulates. Confronts real 2026 data: AI code has 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS vulnerabilities. ARIA's key lesson: "Vibe coding got you here. Agentic engineering gets you to production."

### Act 2 — "First Contact" (Intermediate) — Agentic Engineering
Discovers MCP (agent-to-tool) and A2A (agent-to-agent) — the twin communication protocols. Learns agent architecture (Perceive → Plan → Act → Reflect). Recruits first crew members. Explores both third-party frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen) AND official Agent SDKs (Claude, OpenAI, Google ADK).

### Act 3 — "Fleet Commander" (Advanced) — Production Mastery
Commands a fleet of specialized agent ships (multi-agent orchestration via A2A). Faces the Integration Nebula, deploys HITL safety systems, handles security threats including AI copyright/ethics. Final boss: deploying a production-grade agentic system.

### Epilogue — "The Academy" (Practitioner)
Ship docks at Fleet HQ. Unlocks real-world tooling guides. Space aesthetic continues, real-world content inside. Also accessible from title screen without game progress.

## 3. Tech Stack

| Dependency | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Next.js | 15 (stable) | App Router, SSR/SSG, routing |
| TypeScript | latest | Type safety |
| Tailwind CSS | v4 | CSS-first config via `@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme` |
| Motion | latest | Animations (`motion/react`, NOT framer-motion) |
| HTML5 Canvas | native | Star map, mini-games |
| Howler.js | latest | Audio (ambient loops + SFX sprites, 7kb gzipped) |
| localStorage | native | Game save state (no backend) |
| Vercel | free tier | Hosting + custom domain |

**No backend, no database, no auth.** All state client-side.

### Typography
- Display: Space Grotesk
- Body: Inter
- Mono: JetBrains Mono

### Color System
| Token | Hex | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| Void | `#0a0f1a` | Deep space background |
| Nebula Blue | `#4a6fa5` | Primary UI, MCP content |
| Signal Green | `#6b9e78` | Success, agent content, Plan/Act |
| Core Terracotta | `#c17147` | Warnings, highlights, player actions |
| Starlight | `#e8e0d4` | Text, glowing elements |
| Glass | `rgba(255,255,255,0.05)` | Glassmorphism panels with backdrop-blur |

### Visual Style
Clean minimalist sci-fi. Glassmorphism panels, parallax starfields, SVG planets with orbital rings, spring-physics animations, subtle glow effects. Think *Interstellar* UI meets Linear's design language.

### Audio
Full soundscape: ambient space synth loop + UI SFX (button clicks, warp sounds, mission complete chimes, dialogue bleeps). Synthwave style. Audio opt-in on first interaction (browser requirement).

## 4. Project Structure

```
app/
├── page.tsx                    # Title screen (New Game / Continue / Academy / About)
├── create/                     # Character creation (3 steps)
├── cockpit/                    # Ship HUD — main dashboard
├── starmap/                    # Interactive galaxy map (Canvas)
├── planets/
│   ├── vibe-world/            # Act 1: Vibe coding fundamentals
│   ├── debt-belt/             # Act 1: Tech debt dangers
│   ├── mcp-station/           # Act 2: Model Context Protocol
│   ├── agent-academy/         # Act 2: Agent architecture
│   ├── framework-nebula/      # Act 2: LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen
│   ├── orchestration-citadel/ # Act 3: Multi-agent systems
│   ├── security-fortress/     # Act 3: HITL, local LLMs, security
│   └── production-worlds/     # Act 3: Enterprise deployment
├── academy/                    # Epilogue: Real-world tooling guides
├── inventory/                  # Collected tools/items
└── crew/                       # Recruited agent crew

components/
├── game/
│   ├── StarMap.tsx             # Canvas-based galaxy navigation
│   ├── Cockpit.tsx             # HUD with stats, fuel, crew
│   ├── DialogueSystem.tsx      # NPC conversation engine
│   ├── MissionBriefing.tsx     # Mission intro/outro screens
│   ├── MiniGame.tsx            # Base mini-game wrapper
│   └── Inventory.tsx           # Item management UI
├── ui/
│   ├── GlassPanel.tsx          # Glassmorphism container
│   ├── XPBar.tsx               # Experience progress bar
│   ├── StatGauge.tsx           # Radial stat display
│   ├── TypewriterText.tsx      # Animated text reveal
│   └── WarpTransition.tsx      # Page transition effect
├── audio/
│   └── AudioManager.tsx        # Howler.js wrapper, SFX triggers

lib/
├── game-state.ts               # Save/load, progression logic
├── missions.ts                 # Mission definitions & requirements
├── dialogue-data.ts            # NPC conversation trees
├── items.ts                    # Item/tool definitions
└── crew.ts                     # Crew member definitions & stats

public/
├── audio/
│   ├── ambient-space.mp3
│   └── sfx/                    # UI sounds
├── images/
│   ├── planets/                # SVG/PNG planet illustrations
│   ├── characters/             # NPC portraits
│   ├── items/                  # Inventory icons
│   └── backgrounds/            # Starfields, nebulae
```

# Vibe Voyager — Design Document

> An interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering practices. From beginner to agentic developer.

**URL:** [REDACTED_DOMAIN]
**Hosting:** Vercel (free tier)
**Target:** Lecture demo + standalone learning platform
**Deadline:** ~2026-03-14

---

## 1. Audience

Mixed levels with multiple entry points:
- Software engineering students who code but haven't used AI tools
- Working developers adopting agentic workflows
- Beginners exploring AI-assisted development
- The Academy section is accessible without playing the game (direct access for anyone)

## 2. Narrative Arc

**Key narrative thread:** The game mirrors Karpathy's own evolution — he coined "vibe coding" (Feb 2025), then declared it "passé" and introduced **"agentic engineering"** (Feb 2026). The player lives this arc.

### Act 1 — "The Solo Pilot" (Beginner) — Vibe Coding
Player wakes as a rookie developer in a single-person ship. Learns to fly by talking to ship AI (vibe coding). Fast but fragile — tech debt accumulates. Confronts real 2026 data: AI code has 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS vulnerabilities. ARIA's key lesson: "Vibe coding got you here. Agentic engineering gets you to production."

### Act 2 — "First Contact" (Intermediate) — Agentic Engineering
Discovers MCP (agent-to-tool) and A2A (agent-to-agent) — the twin communication protocols. Learns agent architecture (Perceive → Plan → Act → Reflect). Recruits first crew members. Explores both third-party frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen) AND official Agent SDKs (Claude, OpenAI, Google ADK).

### Act 3 — "Fleet Commander" (Advanced) — Production Mastery
Commands a fleet of specialized agent ships (multi-agent orchestration via A2A). Faces the Integration Nebula, deploys HITL safety systems, handles security threats including AI copyright/ethics. Final boss: deploying a production-grade agentic system.

### Epilogue — "The Academy" (Practitioner)
Ship docks at Fleet HQ. Unlocks real-world tooling guides. Space aesthetic continues, real-world content inside. Also accessible from title screen without game progress.

## 3. Tech Stack

| Dependency | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Next.js | 15 (stable) | App Router, SSR/SSG, routing |
| TypeScript | latest | Type safety |
| Tailwind CSS | v4 | CSS-first config via `@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme` |
| Motion | latest | Animations (`motion/react`, NOT framer-motion) |
| HTML5 Canvas | native | Star map, mini-games |
| Howler.js | latest | Audio (ambient loops + SFX sprites, 7kb gzipped) |
| localStorage | native | Game save state (no backend) |
| Vercel | free tier | Hosting + custom domain |

**No backend, no database, no auth.** All state client-side.

### Typography
- Display: Space Grotesk
- Body: Inter
- Mono: JetBrains Mono

### Color System

# Vibe Voyager — Design Document

> An interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering practices. From beginner to agentic developer.

**URL:** [REDACTED_DOMAIN]
**Hosting:** Vercel (free tier)
**Target:** Lecture demo + standalone learning platform
**Deadline:** ~2026-03-14

---

## 1. Audience

Mixed levels with multiple entry points:
- Software engineering students who code but haven't used AI tools
- Working developers adopting agentic workflows
- Beginners exploring AI-assisted development
- The Academy section is accessible without playing the game (direct access for anyone)

## 2. Narrative Arc

**Key narrative thread:** The game mirrors Karpathy's own evolution — he coined "vibe coding" (Feb 2025), then declared it "passé" and introduced **"agentic engineering"** (Feb 2026). The player lives this arc.

### Act 1 — "The Solo Pilot" (Beginner) — Vibe Coding
Player wakes as a rookie developer in a single-person ship. Learns to fly by talking to ship AI (vibe coding). Fast but fragile — tech debt accumulates. Confronts real 2026 data: AI code has 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS vulnerabilities. ARIA's key lesson: "Vibe coding got you here. Agentic engineering gets you to production."

### Act 2 — "First Contact" (Intermediate) — Agentic Engineering
Discovers MCP (agent-to-tool) and A2A (agent-to-agent) — the twin communication protocols. Learns agent architecture (Perceive → Plan → Act → Reflect). Recruits first crew members. Explores both third-party frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen) AND official Agent SDKs (Claude, OpenAI, Google ADK).

### Act 3 — "Fleet Commander" (Advanced) — Production Mastery
Commands a fleet of specialized agent ships (multi-agent orchestration via A2A). Faces the Integration Nebula, deploys HITL safety systems, handles security threats including AI copyright/ethics. Final boss: deploying a production-grade agentic system.

### Epilogue — "The Academy" (Practitioner)
Ship docks at Fleet HQ. Unlocks real-world tooling guides. Space aesthetic continues, real-world content inside. Also accessible from title screen without game progress.

## 3. Tech Stack

| Dependency | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Next.js | 15 (stable) | App Router, SSR/SSG, routing |
| TypeScript | latest | Type safety |
| Tailwind CSS | v4 | CSS-first config via `@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme` |
| Motion | latest | Animations (`motion/react`, NOT framer-motion) |
| HTML5 Canvas | native | Star map, mini-games |
| Howler.js | latest | Audio (ambient loops + SFX sprites, 7kb gzipped) |
| localStorage | native | Game save state (no backend) |
| Vercel | free tier | Hosting + custom domain |

**No backend, no database, no auth.** All state client-side.

### Typography
- Display: Space Grotesk
- Body: Inter
- Mono: JetBrains Mono

### Color System
| Token | Hex | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| Void | `#0a0f1a` | Deep space background |
| Nebula Blue | `#4a6fa5` | Primary UI, MCP content |
| Signal Green | `#6b9e78` | Success, agent content, Plan/Act |
| Core Terracotta | `#c17147` | Warnings, highlights, player actions |
| Starlight | `#e8e0d4` | Text, glowing elements |
| Glass | `rgba(255,255,255,0.05)` | Glassmorphism panels with backdrop-blur |

### Visual Style
Clean minimalist sci-fi. Glassmorphism panels, parallax starfields, SVG planets with orbital rings, spring-physics animations, subtle glow effects. Think *Interstellar* UI meets Linear's design language.

### Audio
Full soundscape: ambient space synth loop + UI SFX (button clicks, warp sounds, mission complete chimes, dialogue bleeps). Synthwave style. Audio opt-in on first interaction (browser requirement).

# Planet-by-Planet Content Mapping

## ACT 1 — "The Solo Pilot"

### Vibe World (4 missions)
1. "First Words" — What is vibe coding (IBM, Replit, Wikipedia, Google Cloud) → Dialogue
2. "See It, Say It, Run It" — First vibe creation (Slide 2, Beginner Guide) → Prompt Duel
3. "The Prototype Sprint" — Build fast (arXiv: Vibe Coding in Practice) → Timed challenge
4. "Traditional vs. Vibe" — Both paradigms (arXiv: GenAI & Software Dev) → Dialogue/debate

### Debt Asteroid Belt (3 missions)
1. "The Fragile Ship" — Tech debt (Slide 9, Tabnine) → Debug
2. "40% Vulnerable" — Security audit (arXiv, Security Auto Fixer) → Debug/sorting
3. "The Case for Expertise" — Vibe alone isn't enough (Slide 2 quote) → Dialogue quiz, unlocks Act 2

## ACT 2 — "First Contact"

### MCP Station (4 missions)
1. "The N×M Problem" — Integration bottleneck (Slide 4) → Visual puzzle
2. "USB-C for AI" — What MCP is (Slide 5, Anthropic, IBM) → Connect puzzle
3. "Protocol vs. Wrappers" — Comparison (Slide 6) → Dialogue quiz
4. "Docking Sequence" — Hands-on MCP config (Anthropic docs) → Architect

### Agent Academy (5 missions)
1. "The Cognitive Loop" — Agent anatomy (Slide 3) → Architect, recruits Scout
2. "Perception Training" — How agents see (arXiv) → Sorting mini-game
3. "Planning & Reasoning" — Chain of thought (arXiv, Deep Agent article) → Architect tree, recruits Archie
4. "Tool Calling" — How agents act (Akka, ACI) → Connect puzzle
5. "Self-Healing" — Reflect loop (Slide 3 callout) → Debug scenarios, recruits Exec

### Framework Nebula (3 missions)
1. "Three Schools" — LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen (Slide 8, DataCamp) → Dialogue
2. "The Right Tool" — When to use what → Command (drag-drop matching)
3. "Build a Crew" — CrewAI concepts (repos) → Architect fill-in-blank

## ACT 3 — "Fleet Commander"

### Orchestration Citadel (3 missions)
1. "Society of Agents" — Multi-agent pipeline (Slide 7) → Architect
2. "Message Passing" — Agent communication (arXiv, Devin) → Connect puzzle
3. "Delegation" — What to automate (arXiv) → Command triage

### Security Fortress (3 missions)
1. "The Safety Net" — HITL (Slide 10, Galileo) → Architect flowchart, recruits Mirror
2. "Local Defenses" — Local LLMs (Slide 11) → Dialogue quiz
3. "Threat Scan" — Security in agents (Auto Fixer, CWE-95) → Debug

### Production Worlds (3 missions)
1. "Moon Alpha: QE" — Self-healing tests (Slide 12, SWE-bench) → Command
2. "Moon Beta: Enterprise" — Real-world cases (Slide 13, healthcare/BFSI/supply) → Dialogue
3. "Final Mission: Deployment Playbook" — Capstone (Slides 14-15) → Multi-step Architect

## EPILOGUE — "The Academy" (8 Sections)

### Section 1: AI-Powered IDEs & Editors
**GUI IDEs:** Cursor (largest community, highest benchmarks), Google Antigravity (agent-first, Manager Surface, built-in browser), Kiro (AWS, spec-driven, Agent Hooks/Steering), Windsurf (Cognition/Devin, Cascade agent, $15/mo), GitHub Copilot (deepest GitHub integration)
**Terminal Agents:** Claude Code (1M context, skills/plugins), Codex CLI (Rust, multi-agent worktrees, OSS), Gemini CLI (free tier, Google Search grounding, Apache 2.0), Aider (speed, git-aware, OSS)
**VS Code Extensions:** Cline (model-agnostic, governance), Roo Code (role-driven, fast multi-file), Continue (source-controlled AI checks)

### Section 2: AI Code Review & Quality
CodeRabbit (2M+ repos, PR summaries), Greptile (full-codebase graph), Qodo (behavior-focused, test gen), Ellipsis (auto-fix reviewer comments), Cursor BugBot

### Section 3: No-Code / Low-Code Builders
Replit (browser IDE + deploy), Bolt.new (prompt-to-app), Lovable (design quality), v0 by Vercel (UI components)

### Section 4: Claude Code Deep Dive
Installation, CLAUDE.md (global/project/local), skills, plugins, hooks, agent teams, keybindings, MCP servers, best practices cycle

### Section 5: Agentic Development Best Practices
Subagent-driven development, parallelization, AI code review, TDD with agents, memory management, security/HITL, prompt engineering, tech debt management

### Section 6: MCP Workshop
What/why, setting up servers (stdio/HTTP), connecting tools, building your own server, enterprise governance

### Section 7: Resource Library
All 57+ sources from sources.md, organized by topic

### Section 8: How This Was Built
Meta case study from BUILD_LOG.md

## Content Gaps to Fill
- AI tools landscape research → Academy Sections 1-3
- Claude Code deep dive tutorials → Academy Section 4
- Agentic best practices guide → Academy Section 5
- MCP setup walkthrough → Academy Section 6 + MCP Station
- Mini-game interactive content → all challenges
- NPC dialogue scripts → all planets
- Audio assets → global
- Planet/character SVG illustrations → global

3. "The Case for Expertise" — Vibe alone isn't enough (Slide 2 quote) → Dialogue quiz, unlocks Act 2

## ACT 2 — "First Contact"

### MCP Station (4 missions)
1. "The N×M Problem" — Integration bottleneck (Slide 4) → Visual puzzle
2. "USB-C for AI" — What MCP is (Slide 5, Anthropic, IBM) → Connect puzzle
3. "Protocol vs. Wrappers" — Comparison (Slide 6) → Dialogue quiz
4. "Docking Sequence" — Hands-on MCP config (Anthropic docs) → Architect

### Agent Academy (5 missions)
1. "The Cognitive Loop" — Agent anatomy (Slide 3) → Architect, recruits Scout
2. "Perception Training" — How agents see (arXiv) → Sorting mini-game
3. "Planning & Reasoning" — Chain of thought (arXiv, Deep Agent article) → Architect tree, recruits Archie
4. "Tool Calling" — How agents act (Akka, ACI) → Connect puzzle
5. "Self-Healing" — Reflect loop (Slide 3 callout) → Debug scenarios, recruits Exec

### Framework Nebula (3 missions)
1. "Three Schools" — LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen (Slide 8, DataCamp) → Dialogue
2. "The Right Tool" — When to use what → Command (drag-drop matching)
3. "Build a Crew" — CrewAI concepts (repos) → Architect fill-in-blank

1. "Society of Agents" — Multi-agent pipeline (Slide 7) → Architect
2. "Message Passing" — Agent communication (arXiv, Devin) → Connect puzzle

2. "Local Defenses" — Local LLMs (Slide 11) → Dialogue quiz
3. "Threat Scan" — Security in agents (Auto Fixer, CWE-95) → Debug

1. "Moon Alpha: QE" — Self-healing tests (Slide 12, SWE-bench) → Command
2. "Moon Beta: Enterprise" — Real-world cases (Slide 13, healthcare/BFSI/supply) → Dialogue
3. "Final Mission: Deployment Playbook" — Capstone (Slides 14-15) → Multi-step Architect

### Section 1: AI-Powered IDEs & Editors
**GUI IDEs:** Cursor (largest community, highest benchmarks), Google Antigravity (agent-first, Manager Surface, built-in browser), Kiro (AWS, spec-driven, Agent Hooks/Steering), Windsurf (Cognition/Devin, Cascade agent, $15/mo), GitHub Copilot (deepest GitHub integration)
**Terminal Agents:** Claude Code (1M context, skills/plugins), Codex CLI (Rust, multi-agent worktrees, OSS), Gemini CLI (free tier, Google Search grounding, Apache 2.0), Aider (speed, git-aware, OSS)

CodeRabbit (2M+ repos, PR summaries), Greptile (full-codebase graph), Qodo (behavior-focused, test gen), Ellipsis (auto-fix reviewer comments), Cursor BugBot

Replit (browser IDE + deploy), Bolt.new (prompt-to-app), Lovable (design quality), v0 by Vercel (UI components)

Installation, CLAUDE.md (global/project/local), skills, plugins, hooks, agent teams, keybindings, MCP servers, best practices cycle

### Section 5: Agentic Development Best Practices
Subagent-driven development, parallelization, AI code review, TDD with agents, memory management, security/HITL, prompt engineering, tech debt management

### Section 6: MCP Workshop
What/why, setting up servers (stdio/HTTP), connecting tools, building your own server, enterprise governance

All 57+ sources from sources.md, organized by topic

Meta case study from BUILD_LOG.md

**Narrative gap for your game:** You need a "philosophical foundation" level early in the journey that addresses learner anxiety ("Will I be replaced?") head-on. The answer is: *what you're learning to DO is changing, but the need for people who can THINK about systems is growing.*

**Key sources to verify/update:**
- Stack Overflow annual developer surveys (2024, 2025)
- Kent Beck's Substack posts on AI and software design
- Steve Yegge's "AI-assisted coding" essays on sourcegraph.com
- GitHub's "State of the Octoverse" reports

---

### GAP 2: The New Role Taxonomy

**Emerging titles and roles (2024-2025):**
- **AI Engineer** -- a distinct role popularized by Shawn "@swyx" Wang and the AI Engineer Summit (2023-2024). Not an ML engineer, not a traditional SWE -- someone who builds products on top of foundation models using APIs, RAG, fine-tuning, and prompt engineering.
- **Prompt Engineer** -- peaked in 2023, now largely absorbed into other roles rather than standing alone.
- **Agent Developer / Agentic Developer** -- building autonomous AI systems that can take actions, use tools, and complete multi-step workflows.
- **AI Infrastructure Engineer** -- focused on the deployment stack: model serving, GPU orchestration, observability for AI systems.
- **LLMOps / MLOps Engineer** -- operationalizing LLM-based systems (evaluation, monitoring, cost management, guardrails).
- **AI Product Manager** -- understanding what AI can/can't do to scope products realistically.
- **Vibe Coder** (informal) -- Andrej Karpathy coined this in early 2025, referring to non-traditional developers who build by describing intent and iterating with AI.

**Narrative gap:** Your game should have a "career map" or "skill tree" that shows these branching paths. A beginner doesn't just become an "agentic developer" -- they could specialize in multiple directions. The game should make these paths visible.

**Key sources:**
- Swyx's "The Rise of the AI Engineer" (latent.space, 2023)
- Andrej Karpathy's tweet coining "vibe coding" (Feb 2025)
- Chip Huyen's writing on ML/AI engineering roles
- AI Engineer Summit recordings (2023, 2024)

---

### GAP 3: The New Skills Stack

**Skills that barely existed in 2023 but are essential by 2025-2026:**

| Skill | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|
| **Prompt Engineering (structured)** | Not just "asking nicely" -- understanding chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, system prompts, structured output formats |
| **Context Window Management** | Knowing what to put in (and leave out of) an LLM's context. This is a genuine engineering skill. |
| **Agent Orchestration** | Designing multi-step agentic workflows, tool use, error recovery, human-in-the-loop patterns |
| **Evaluation & Benchmarking** | Writing evals for LLM outputs. "Vibes-based" testing is insufficient -- you need systematic evaluation frameworks |
| **RAG Architecture** | Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking strategies, embedding models, vector databases, hybrid search |
| **Guardrails & Safety Engineering** | Output filtering, content policies, jailbreak prevention, responsible AI deployment |
| **AI-Aware System Design** | Designing architectures that account for non-determinism, latency, cost, and failure modes of AI components |
| **Cost Engineering for AI** | Token economics, caching strategies, model selection tradeoffs (GPT-4 vs smaller models) |
| **MCP & Tool-Use Protocol Design** | Designing clean interfaces for AI agents to interact with external systems |
| **Reading & Understanding AI Code** | Reviewing AI-generated code is now a bigger part of the job than writing code from scratch |

**Narrative gap:** Your game likely covers prompt engineering and MCP, but may be missing: **evaluation as a core discipline**, **context management as an engineering skill**, and **cost engineering**. These are the unglamorous but critical skills that separate a vibe coder from a production-ready agentic developer.

**Key sources:**
- Anthropic's documentation on prompt engineering best practices
- Hamel Husain's writing on LLM evaluation (hamel.dev)
- Jason Wei et al., "Chain-of-Thought Prompting" (Google, 2022)
- LangChain / LangSmith documentation on evaluation

---

### GAP 4: How Code Review Has Changed

**The new review workflow (emerging 2024-2025):**

1. **AI writes first draft** (Copilot, Cursor, Claude, etc.)
2. **Human reviews AI output** -- this is now the primary developer activity for many teams. The skill shifts from "can I write this?" to "is this correct, secure, performant, and maintainable?"
3. **AI-assisted review** -- tools like GitHub Copilot for Pull Requests, CodeRabbit, and Graphite's AI review provide automated review comments.
4. **The "double AI" problem** -- AI generates code, AI reviews code, and humans become a rubber stamp. This is an active concern.

**New code review skills needed:**
- **Spotting plausible-but-wrong code** -- AI-generated code often LOOKS correct. The bugs are subtle: off-by-one errors, incorrect edge case handling, hallucinated API methods, insecure defaults.
- **Reviewing for style drift** -- AI code can be stylistically inconsistent with the codebase.
- **Checking for license contamination** -- did the AI reproduce copyrighted/licensed code?
- **Verifying AI-suggested dependencies** -- AI sometimes suggests packages that don't exist (dependency confusion) or are outdated/vulnerable.

**Narrative gap:** Your game should have a dedicated module on "AI Code Review" as a skill. This is arguably the MOST important skill for a developer in 2026 -- the ability to critically evaluate code you didn't write and may not fully understand at first glance. Include exercises where learners must find bugs in AI-generated code.

**Key sources:**
- GitHub's Copilot impact studies
- GitClear's 2024 report on AI code quality ("Code Quality in the AI Era")
- Google's research on code review practices
- CodeRabbit, Graphite documentation on AI-assisted review

---

### GAP 5: AI-Generated Code Quality -- The Evidence

**What studies have found (2024-2025):**

- **GitClear (Jan 2024):** Found that code churn (code that is written and then quickly rewritten or deleted) increased significantly in repos using AI coding tools, suggesting AI-generated code may have lower durability.
- **Stanford/UIUC study (2023):** Developers using AI assistants wrote code with MORE security vulnerabilities, and were MORE confident in their code's security -- a dangerous combination.
- **GitHub's own research (2024):** Showed productivity gains (faster task completion) but acknowledged quality metrics need more study.
- **Google DeepMind (2024-2025):** Published research on AI's ability to find and fix bugs, showing promising but imperfect results.
- **Snyk (2024-2025):** Reported on security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, finding significant rates of insecure patterns.

**The emerging picture:** AI code is "good enough for the middle" -- straightforward CRUD operations, boilerplate, standard patterns. It struggles with: edge cases, security-sensitive code, novel algorithms, and code that requires deep domain knowledge.

**Narrative gap:** Your game needs a "trust but verify" module that teaches learners when to trust AI output and when to be skeptical. Include real examples of AI-generated bugs and security vulnerabilities. This is critical for the journey from "vibe coding" (where you accept AI output) to "agentic development" (where you build systems that are reliable).

**Key sources:**
- GitClear, "Coding on Copilot: 2023 Data Suggests Downward Pressure on Code Quality" (Jan 2024)
- Perry et al., "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" (Stanford, 2023)
- Snyk's AI code security reports
- GitHub's Copilot productivity research

---

### GAP 6: The Company Transition -- What "AI-Native" Looks Like

**Patterns emerging in 2024-2025:**

- **"AI-first" development workflows:** Companies like Vercel, Replit, and Cognition (Devin) are building entire development environments around AI as the primary interface.
- **The "10x solo developer" thesis:** Small teams (or even individuals) can now build and maintain products that previously required 20+ engineers. This is changing startup economics.
- **Internal AI coding platforms:** Large enterprises (Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon) have internal AI coding tools that are more deeply integrated than public tools.
- **"Shift left" with AI:** AI is being integrated earlier in the SDLC -- requirements analysis, design review, test generation -- not just code completion.
- **New deployment risks:** Companies must manage model versioning, prompt versioning, evaluation pipelines, and AI-specific incident response.
- **The "shadow AI" problem:** Developers using unauthorized AI tools, creating security and IP risks.

**Narrative gap:** Your game should include a "team & org" dimension. The journey isn't just individual skill development -- it's about how you work within an organization that's adopting AI. Include scenarios about: convincing a team to adopt AI tools, managing AI-generated technical debt, setting up AI coding policies.

**Key sources:**
- a16z's "AI in the Enterprise" reports
- Sequoia Capital's AI market analyses
- Replit's blog on AI-native development
- Cognition AI's Devin launch and subsequent industry response

---

### GAP 7: Ethics, Copyright, and Environmental Impact

**Active issues (2024-2026):**

- **Copyright:** The *New York Times v. OpenAI* lawsuit (filed Dec 2023, ongoing) is the landmark case. Multiple lawsuits from artists and authors are ongoing. The legal landscape is deeply unsettled. The EU AI Act (effective 2025-2026) requires transparency about training data.
- **License laundering:** AI trained on GPL-licensed code generating output that companies use in proprietary products. The legal status is unresolved.
- **Bias in AI-generated code:** AI can perpetuate biases in variable naming, algorithmic choices (e.g., defaulting to binary gender), accessibility oversights, and cultural assumptions in UX code.
- **Environmental impact:** Training large models requires massive energy. GPT-4 training was estimated at ~$100M in compute. The ongoing inference costs for millions of developers using AI coding tools are substantial. Water usage for data center cooling is an emerging concern.
- **The "homogenization" risk:** If everyone uses the same AI tools, codebases converge on similar patterns, potentially reducing diversity of approaches and creating monoculture vulnerabilities.
- **Attribution and credit:** Who "wrote" AI-assisted code? How do open-source contribution norms change?

**Narrative gap:** Your game should have an ethics module that isn't a bolt-on afterthought but is woven through the journey. At the "vibe coding" stage, introduce license awareness. At the "agentic developer" stage, introduce responsible AI system design. Include dilemmas where learners must make ethical choices.

**Key sources:**
- NYT v. OpenAI court filings
- EU AI Act text and analyses
- AI Now Institute reports
- Sasha Luccioni's research on AI environmental impact (Hugging Face)
- Software Freedom Conservancy's positions on AI and copyleft

---

### GAP 8: What Junior Developers Need to Learn Differently

**The fundamental shift:**

The traditional junior developer learning path was: learn syntax -> build small projects -> understand data structures & algorithms -> get a job -> learn the codebase -> contribute small fixes -> grow.

**The new path emerging in 2025-2026:**

1. **Learn to read code before writing it.** AI generates code, so the first skill is understanding and evaluating code you didn't write.
2. **Learn systems thinking early.** With AI handling syntax, juniors can engage with architecture and design patterns much sooner.
3. **Learn debugging and testing as primary skills.** Not afterthoughts -- these are now the core of what humans do.
4. **Develop a "bullshit detector" for AI output.** Learn to recognize when AI is confidently wrong, hallucinating APIs, or generating plausible-but-incorrect logic.
5. **Learn version control and collaboration deeply.** AI makes it easy to generate code but doesn't help with the social/organizational aspects of software development.
6. **Build mental models, not just muscle memory.** Understanding WHY code works (not just THAT it works) is critical when you're reviewing AI output.
7. **The "tutorial hell 2.0" risk:** Instead of being stuck watching tutorials, juniors can get stuck in "prompt hell" -- iterating with AI without building understanding.

**The junior developer crisis:** There's a genuine concern that juniors are being cut from hiring pipelines because AI replaces the tasks traditionally given to juniors (simple bug fixes, boilerplate code). This creates a pipeline problem -- how do you develop senior engineers if no one goes through the junior phase?

**Narrative gap:** This is potentially the BIGGEST gap in your game. Your audience (beginners) needs to hear: "Yes, AI changes how you learn, but you MUST still build deep understanding. Here's how." Include a "learning how to learn with AI" meta-module. Address the anxiety about junior roles disappearing. Show how AI can actually ACCELERATE the learning process if used correctly (AI as tutor, not as crutch).

**Key sources:**
- Addy Osmani's posts on junior developer growth with AI (2024-2025)
- ThePrimeagen's content on the junior developer problem
- Cal Newport's writing on deep work in the AI era
- Various HackerNews discussions on junior hiring freezes

---

## Summary: Top 10 Narrative Gaps (Prioritized)

| Priority | Gap | Why It Matters for Your Game |
|----------|-----|------------------------------|
| 1 | **"Learning to Learn with AI" meta-skill** | Your audience is beginners -- they need guidance on how to use AI WITHOUT becoming dependent |
| 2 | **Code review as a primary skill** | The #1 activity for developers in 2026; missing entirely from most learning paths |
| 3 | **Evaluation & testing AI systems** | The bridge between "vibe coding" and "production-ready"; likely underrepresented in your content |
| 4 | **The trust calibration problem** | When to trust AI, when to verify, when to reject -- this is the core judgment skill |
| 5 | **Career path visibility** | Show learners the branching paths (AI Engineer, Agent Developer, AI Infra, etc.) |
| 6 | **Cost & context engineering** | Unglamorous but essential production skills missing from most curricula |
| 7 | **Ethics woven through, not bolted on** | Copyright, bias, and environmental concerns should appear at each stage |
| 8 | **The junior developer pipeline crisis** | Address the elephant in the room -- learners need to know the landscape honestly |
| 9 | **Organizational/team dynamics** | How AI changes team structure, not just individual productivity |
| 10 | **The philosophical foundation** | Address "is SE dead?" anxiety upfront to motivate the rest of the journey |

---

- The latest Stack Overflow Developer Survey (2025 edition)
- GitHub's Octoverse 2025 report
- Any landmark court rulings in AI copyright cases
- New AI coding tools or paradigm shifts announced after mid-2025
- The current state of the EU AI Act enforcement
- Whether new role titles have emerged beyond what I've listed

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/dev/[REDACTED_PROJECT]

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For Claude:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

**Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

**Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

**Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

**Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (this session)** - I dispatch fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Parallel Session (separate)** - Open new session with executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Stay in this session
- Fresh subagent per task + code review

**If Parallel Session chosen:**
- Guide them to open new session in worktree
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** New session uses superpowers:executing-plans

I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan.

Let me first review the design doc and project structure to write a comprehensive plan.

# Vibe Voyager — Design Document

> An interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering practices. From beginner to agentic developer.

**URL:** [REDACTED_DOMAIN]
**Hosting:** Vercel (free tier)
**Target:** Lecture demo + standalone learning platform
**Deadline:** ~2026-03-14

---

## 1. Audience

Mixed levels with multiple entry points:
- Software engineering students who code but haven't used AI tools
- Working developers adopting agentic workflows
- Beginners exploring AI-assisted development
- The Academy section is accessible without playing the game (direct access for anyone)

## 2. Narrative Arc

**Key narrative thread:** The game mirrors Karpathy's own evolution — he coined "vibe coding" (Feb 2025), then declared it "passé" and introduced **"agentic engineering"** (Feb 2026). The player lives this arc.

### Act 1 — "The Solo Pilot" (Beginner) — Vibe Coding
Player wakes as a rookie developer in a single-person ship. Learns to fly by talking to ship AI (vibe coding). Fast but fragile — tech debt accumulates. Confronts real 2026 data: AI code has 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS vulnerabilities. ARIA's key lesson: "Vibe coding got you here. Agentic engineering gets you to production."

### Act 2 — "First Contact" (Intermediate) — Agentic Engineering
Discovers MCP (agent-to-tool) and A2A (agent-to-agent) — the twin communication protocols. Learns agent architecture (Perceive → Plan → Act → Reflect). Recruits first crew members. Explores both third-party frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen) AND official Agent SDKs (Claude, OpenAI, Google ADK).

### Act 3 — "Fleet Commander" (Advanced) — Production Mastery
Commands a fleet of specialized agent ships (multi-agent orchestration via A2A). Faces the Integration Nebula, deploys HITL safety systems, handles security threats including AI copyright/ethics. Final boss: deploying a production-grade agentic system.

### Epilogue — "The Academy" (Practitioner)
Ship docks at Fleet HQ. Unlocks real-world tooling guides. Space aesthetic continues, real-world content inside. Also accessible from title screen without game progress.

## 3. Tech Stack

| Dependency | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Next.js | 15 (stable) | App Router, SSR/SSG, routing |
| TypeScript | latest | Type safety |
| Tailwind CSS | v4 | CSS-first config via `@import "tailwindcss"` and `@theme` |
| Motion | latest | Animations (`motion/react`, NOT framer-motion) |
| HTML5 Canvas | native | Star map, mini-games |
| Howler.js | latest | Audio (ambient loops + SFX sprites, 7kb gzipped) |
| localStorage | native | Game save state (no backend) |
| Vercel | free tier | Hosting + custom domain |

**No backend, no database, no auth.** All state client-side.

### Typography
- Display: Space Grotesk
- Body: Inter
- Mono: JetBrains Mono

### Color System
| Token | Hex | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| Void | `#0a0f1a` | Deep space background |
| Nebula Blue | `#4a6fa5` | Primary UI, MCP content |
| Signal Green | `#6b9e78` | Success, agent content, Plan/Act |
| Core Terracotta | `#c17147` | Warnings, highlights, player actions |
| Starlight | `#e8e0d4` | Text, glowing elements |
| Glass | `rgba(255,255,255,0.05)` | Glassmorphism panels with backdrop-blur |

### Visual Style
Clean minimalist sci-fi. Glassmorphism panels, parallax starfields, SVG planets with orbital rings, spring-physics animations, subtle glow effects. Think *Interstellar* UI meets Linear's design language.

### Audio
Full soundscape: ambient space synth loop + UI SFX (button clicks, warp sounds, mission complete chimes, dialogue bleeps). Synthwave style. Audio opt-in on first interaction (browser requirement).

## 4. Project Structure

```
app/
├── page.tsx                    # Title screen (New Game / Continue / Academy / About)
├── create/                     # Character creation (3 steps)
├── cockpit/                    # Ship HUD — main dashboard
├── starmap/                    # Interactive galaxy map (Canvas)
├── planets/
│   ├── vibe-world/            # Act 1: Vibe coding fundamentals
│   ├── debt-belt/             # Act 1: Tech debt dangers
│   ├── mcp-station/           # Act 2: Model Context Protocol
│   ├── agent-academy/         # Act 2: Agent architecture
│   ├── framework-nebula/      # Act 2: LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen
│   ├── orchestration-citadel/ # Act 3: Multi-agent systems
│   ├── security-fortress/     # Act 3: HITL, local LLMs, security
│   └── production-worlds/     # Act 3: Enterprise deployment
├── academy/                    # Epilogue: Real-world tooling guides
├── inventory/                  # Collected tools/items
└── crew/                       # Recruited agent crew

components/
├── game/
│   ├── StarMap.tsx             # Canvas-based galaxy navigation
│   ├── Cockpit.tsx             # HUD with stats, fuel, crew
│   ├── DialogueSystem.tsx      # NPC conversation engine
│   ├── MissionBriefing.tsx     # Mission intro/outro screens
│   ├── MiniGame.tsx            # Base mini-game wrapper
│   └── Inventory.tsx           # Item management UI
├── ui/
│   ├── GlassPanel.tsx          # Glassmorphism container
│   ├── XPBar.tsx               # Experience progress bar
│   ├── StatGauge.tsx           # Radial stat display
│   ├── TypewriterText.tsx      # Animated text reveal
│   └── WarpTransition.tsx      # Page transition effect
├── audio/
│   └── AudioManager.tsx        # Howler.js wrapper, SFX triggers

lib/
├── game-state.ts               # Save/load, progression logic
├── missions.ts                 # Mission definitions & requirements
├── dialogue-data.ts            # NPC conversation trees
├── items.ts                    # Item/tool definitions
└── crew.ts                     # Crew member definitions & stats

public/
├── audio/
│   ├── ambient-space.mp3
│   └── sfx/                    # UI sounds
├── images/
│   ├── planets/                # SVG/PNG planet illustrations
│   ├── characters/             # NPC portraits
│   ├── items/                  # Inventory icons
│   └── backgrounds/            # Starfields, nebulae
```

## 5. Game Systems

### Player Stats (4 stats, each 1–10)
| Stat | Represents | Leveled by |

| Vibe | Natural language fluency with AI | Vibe coding missions, prompt challenges |
| Architecture | System design & agent thinking | Agent anatomy, framework comparisons |
| Protocol | Integration & MCP knowledge | MCP missions, connection challenges |
| Command | Leadership of multi-agent systems | Orchestration missions, fleet exercises |

### Ranks (combined stat total)
| Rank | Total | Unlocks |
|---|---|---|
| Cadet | 4–10 | Act 1 |
| Navigator | 11–20 | Act 2 |
| Commander | 21–30 | Act 3 |
| Admiral | 31–40 | Academy (also accessible from title screen) |

### Character Creation
1. Choose callsign (text input)
2. Choose ship (3 cosmetic SVG silhouettes: The Spark, The Architect, The Sentinel)
3. Intro text crawl → [ LAUNCH ] → warp into cockpit

### Mission Structure
Each planet has 3–5 missions. Each mission follows: **Briefing → Learning Phase → Challenge → Debrief**

### Challenge Types
| Type | Mechanic |
|---|---|
| Prompt Duel | Write best natural language prompt, scored on completeness |
| Architect | Drag-and-drop nodes to build system diagrams |
| Connect | Draw connections in visual puzzle (MCP wiring) |
| Debug | Find problems in code/architecture scenarios |
| Command | Assign right agents to right tasks |
| Dialogue | NPC quiz-conversations with branching answers |

### Crew System (maps to Perceive → Plan → Act → Reflect)
| Member | Role | Recruited at |
|---|---|---|
| ARIA | Ship AI / narrator | Start of game |
| Scout | Perception specialist | Agent Academy M1 |
| Archie | Planning / reasoning | Agent Academy M3 |
| Exec | Action / execution | Agent Academy M5 |
| Mirror | Reflection / testing | Security Fortress M1 |

### Inventory
Items = real tools with in-game names. Each has a description card explaining the real-world tool.
- Ship Voice Module (Claude Code / Cursor)
- Context Adapter (MCP)
- Agent Blueprint (Agent architecture pattern)
- Fleet Comm Array (Multi-agent orchestration)
- Security Shield (HITL framework)
- Local Core (Ollama / Local LLMs)
- Skill Chips (Claude Code skills/plugins)

### Save System
- Auto-save to localStorage after every mission
- No password gating — progression earned through completion
- "New Game" reset option

## 6. Planet-by-Planet Content Map

### ACT 1 — "The Solo Pilot"

**Vibe World** (4 missions)
1. "First Words" — What is vibe coding → Dialogue quiz (sources: IBM, Replit, Wikipedia, Google Cloud)
2. "See It, Say It, Run It" — First vibe creation → Prompt Duel (sources: Slide 2, Beginner Guide)
3. "The Prototype Sprint" — Build fast → Timed challenge (source: arXiv Vibe Coding in Practice)
4. "Traditional vs. Vibe" — Both paradigms → Debate dialogue (source: arXiv GenAI & Software Dev)

**Debt Asteroid Belt** (4 missions)
1. "The Fragile Ship" — Tech debt → Debug 5 problems (sources: Slide 9, Tabnine)
2. "The Quality Crisis" — 2026 data: 1.75x more bugs, 2.74x more XSS, 4x more code cloning → Debug real vulnerability types (sources: CodeRabbit report, Black Duck OSSRA 2026)
3. "Your Career in the AI Era" — Harvard study: junior dev employment drops 9-10%, BUT AI unlocks new domains → Dialogue with career counselor NPC (sources: Harvard study, Stack Overflow)
4. "The Case for Expertise" — Why vibe alone isn't enough, transition to agentic engineering → Dialogue quiz, Karpathy quote, unlocks Act 2

### ACT 2 — "First Contact"

**MCP Station** (5 missions)
1. "The N×M Problem" — Integration bottleneck → Visual puzzle (source: Slide 4)
2. "USB-C for AI" — What MCP is, 97M monthly downloads, Linux Foundation governance → Connect puzzle (sources: Slide 5, Anthropic, IBM, Context Studios)
3. "Protocol vs. Wrappers" — Comparison, MCP 1.0 targeting June 2026 → Dialogue quiz (source: Slide 6)
4. "Docking Sequence" — MCP hands-on config → Architect JSON blocks (source: Anthropic docs)
5. "The Babel Problem" — Intro to A2A: agents can use tools (MCP) but can't talk to each other. Discovery of Agent-to-Agent protocol → Connect puzzle wiring agents together (sources: Google A2A blog, Linux Foundation)

**Agent Academy** (5 missions)
1. "The Cognitive Loop" — Agent anatomy → Architect cycle + recruit Scout (source: Slide 3)
2. "Perception Training" — How agents see → Sorting mini-game (source: arXiv)
3. "Planning & Reasoning" — Chain of thought → Tree decomposition + recruit Archie (source: Deep Agent article)
4. "Tool Calling" — How agents act → Connect puzzle (sources: Akka, ACI)
5. "Self-Healing" — Reflect loop → Debug scenarios + recruit Exec (source: Slide 3)

**Framework Nebula** (5 missions)
1. "Three Schools of Thought" — Framework overview: LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen → NPC dialogues (source: Slide 8, DataCamp)
2. "The Official Armories" — Vendor Agent SDKs: Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK → Comparison dialogue + Architect (sources: Anthropic docs, OpenAI docs, Google ADK docs)
3. "The Right Tool" — When to use what (frameworks vs SDKs vs custom) → Command matching (source: DataCamp, ClickHouse comparison)
4. "Build a Crew" — CrewAI concepts → Architect fill-in-blank (sources: CrewAI, CAMEL repos)
5. "Agent Cards" — A2A capability discovery, AGENTS.md configuration → Architect: build an Agent Card JSON (sources: A2A protocol docs, AGENTS.md spec)

### ACT 3 — "Fleet Commander"

**Orchestration Citadel** (4 missions)
1. "Society of Agents" — Multi-agent pipeline → Architect nodes (source: Slide 7)
2. "The A2A Network" — A2A protocol deep dive: capability discovery, task delegation, artifact exchange between agents. 72% of enterprise projects now use multi-agent architectures → Connect routing with Agent Cards (sources: Google A2A blog, FrankX roadmap)
3. "Message Passing" — Agent communication patterns → Connect routing (sources: arXiv, Devin blog)
4. "Delegation" — What to automate (87% of Fortune 500 use AI coding tools) → Command triage (sources: arXiv, Second Talent stats)

**Security Fortress** (4 missions)
1. "The Safety Net" — HITL → Architect flowchart + recruit Mirror (sources: Slide 10, Galileo)
2. "Local Defenses" — Local LLMs → Dialogue quiz (source: Slide 11)
3. "Threat Scan" — Security vulnerabilities → Debug challenge (sources: Auto Fixer, CWE-95, Black Duck OSSRA 2026)
4. "The Legal Frontier" — AI copyright, licensing, open-source attribution, disclosure rules. Mirror raises the concerns → Dialogue quiz (sources: U.S. Copyright Office, Red Hat legal analysis)

**Production Worlds** (3 missions — three moons)
1. "Moon Alpha: Quality Engineering" — Self-healing tests → Command (sources: Slide 12, SWE-bench)
2. "Moon Beta: The Enterprise" — Real-world cases → Dialogue quiz (source: Slides 12-13)
3. "Final Mission: Deployment Playbook" — Capstone → Multi-step Architect (sources: Slides 14-15)

## 7. The Academy (Epilogue + Direct Access)

Accessible from title screen without game progress. Space aesthetic continues, real-world content inside glassmorphism panels with terminal-style code blocks.

### Section 1: AI-Powered IDEs & Editors

#### GUI-Based IDEs
| Tool | Developer | Key Differentiator | Pricing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cursor** | Anysphere | Largest community, highest benchmark scores, tab completions + agent mode | $20/mo Pro |
| **Google Antigravity** | Google | Agent-first platform, Manager Surface for multi-agent orchestration, built-in browser testing | Free preview |
| **Kiro** | AWS | Spec-driven development, Agent Hooks for automation, Agent Steering docs | Free preview |
| **Windsurf** | Cognition (Devin) | Cascade agent anticipates next moves, best value at $15/mo | $15/mo Pro |
| **GitHub Copilot** | GitHub/Microsoft | Deepest GitHub integration, workspace agents, code review built-in | $10/mo |

#### Terminal-Native Agents
| Tool | Developer | Key Differentiator | Pricing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Anthropic | 1M token context, deepest reasoning, skills/plugins/hooks ecosystem | $20/mo Pro, $100-200/mo Teams |
| **Codex CLI** | OpenAI | Rust-built, multi-agent with worktrees, MCP support, open source | Usage-based |
| **Gemini CLI** | Google | 1M token context, free tier (60 req/min), Google Search grounding, open source (Apache 2.0) | Free / usage-based |
| **Aider** | Paul Gauthier | Speed-focused, multi-file changes via natural language, git-aware, open source | Free (OSS) |

#### VS Code Extensions (Open Source)
| Tool | Key Differentiator |
|---|---|
| **Cline** | Model-agnostic, stepwise Plan→Act pipeline, full audit trail, governance-focused |
| **Roo Code** | Cline fork, role-driven execution modes (architect/tester), faster on large multi-file changes |
| **Continue** | Open-source autopilot, source-controlled AI checks on PRs |

#### Other Notable Tools
| Tool | Developer | Key Differentiator |
|---|---|---|
| **JetBrains AI** | JetBrains | Built into IntelliJ/PyCharm/WebStorm ecosystem |
| **Amazon Q Developer** | AWS | Security scanning, code transformation, AWS-native |
| **Tabnine** | Tabnine | Privacy-focused, runs locally, enterprise-grade |
| **Sourcegraph Cody** | Sourcegraph | Universal codebase context, cross-repo awareness |

### Section 2: AI Code Review & Quality Tools

| Tool | What It Does |
|---|---|
| **CodeRabbit** | AI PR reviewer on GitHub/GitLab, 2M+ repos connected, auto-summaries and walkthroughs |
| **Greptile** | Full-codebase graph analysis for cross-file bug detection |
| **Qodo** | Behavior-focused review, auto-generates test suites, persistent codebase intelligence |
| **Ellipsis** | Auto-generates fixes for reviewer comments, reduces review cycles |
| **Cursor BugBot** | Automated bug detection integrated into Cursor IDE |

### Section 3: No-Code / Low-Code Builders

| Tool | What It Does |
|---|---|
| **Replit** | Browser-based IDE with AI agent, deploy in one click |
| **Bolt.new** | Prompt-to-app builder, full-stack in browser |
| **Lovable** | AI app builder focused on design quality |
| **v0 by Vercel** | UI component generator from prompts, React + Tailwind output |

### Section 4: Agent SDKs & Protocols
Building your own agents with official vendor SDKs:
- **Claude Agent SDK** (Python + TypeScript) — same tools as Claude Code, programmable, MCP-native

### Section 8: Resource Library

- The brainstorming process
- Planning with skills

### Section 10: Career Paths
Mapping game skills to real-world roles emerging in 2026:
- **AI-Native Developer** — builds with AI as default, not afterthought
- **AI Full-Stack Developer** — applications where AI is core architecture (LLMs, vector stores, agent systems in every layer)
- **Prompt Engineer** — specialist in crafting AI prompts for production systems
- **Agentic Engineer** — Karpathy's term: orchestrates AI agents who write 99% of the code, with human oversight
- Which game skills map to which roles
- Entry points and learning paths for each

## 8. UX Flow

### Title Screen
Slow-drifting parallax starfield. Nebula gradient pulses gently.

```
         V I B E   V O Y A G E R
         The Agentic Coding Odyssey

         [  N E W   G A M E  ]
         [  C O N T I N U E  ]
         [  A C A D E M Y    ]
         [  A B O U T        ]
```

- Ambient audio starts on first interaction
- "Continue" grayed out if no save exists
- "Academy" always accessible (no game progress required)

### Core Navigation Loop
```
Star Map ──select planet──→ Planet (missions) ──complete/return──→ Cockpit (HUD home)
   ↑                                                                      │
   └──────────────────────── open star map ───────────────────────────────┘
```

### Persistent Nav Bar (bottom, cockpit-styled)
Star Map | Cockpit (home) | Crew | Inventory | Academy | Audio Toggle

### Star Map (Canvas)
- 3-layer parallax starfield
- Planets as glowing spheres with orbital ring animations
- 3 visible regions: Act 1 (warm, center), Act 2 (cool, frontier), Act 3 (dramatic, edge)
- Academy space station always visible at top
- Planet states: Locked (dim) → Available (pulsing) → In Progress (partial ring) → Completed (full glow + badge)

### Cockpit HUD
Glassmorphism panels on starfield:
- Callsign + Rank
- 4 stat gauges (radial/horizontal bars with glow)
- Crew portraits (silhouette with "?" for unrecruited)
- Mission log (current objective + overall progress)
- Recent inventory items

### Page Transitions
- Star Map → Planet: Stars streak toward center (warp in)
- Planet → Cockpit: Gentle fade with HUD boot-up flicker
- Cockpit → Star Map: Reverse warp (stars expand outward)
- Mission complete: Flash of light → debrief slides in
- All via Motion `AnimatePresence` with custom variants

### Mobile Responsiveness
- Star map: scrollable/zoomable touch canvas
- Cockpit: stacks vertically
- Dialogue: already mobile-friendly (text + buttons)
- Mini-games: tap instead of click/drag
- Nav bar: fixed bottom (thumb-friendly)

## 9. Content Gaps to Create

| Gap | Location | Source |
|---|---|---|
| AI tools landscape (IDEs, agents, review tools) | Academy Sections 1-3 | Research + first-hand experience |
| Claude Code deep dive tutorials | Academy Section 4 | Written from experience |
| Agentic best practices guide | Academy Section 5 | Nexus/Continuum workflows |
| MCP setup walkthrough | Academy Section 6 | Anthropic docs |
| Mini-game interactive content | All challenge missions | Built as game mechanics |
| NPC dialogue scripts | All planets | Written from source material |
| Audio assets | Global | Royalty-free / generated |
| Planet/character SVG illustrations | Global | AI-generated or designed |

## 10. Build Approach

- **Framework:** Superpowers plugin workflow (brainstorm → plan → execute → review)
- **Execution:** Subagent-driven development with parallel agent teams
- **Quality:** Compound engineering review agents between phases
- **Tracking:** BUILD_LOG.md updated after every major milestone
- **Verification:** verification-before-completion skill before any "done" claim
- **Docs:** Context7 for all library API verification before writing code

---

*Design approved 2026-03-07. Ready for implementation planning.*

- No password gating — progression earned through completion
- "New Game" reset option

1. The user wants to use agent teams for parallel execution
2. They've done 50k+ lines in 2 days before
3. Deadline is ~1 week from March 7, 2026
4. Stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Motion, Canvas, Howler.js
5. No backend — all localStorage

Let me think about the build phases and what can be parallelized:

**Phase 1: Scaffolding (sequential — foundation)**


Setting up the Next.js 15 project with dependencies, Tailwind v4 design tokens, fonts, and base layout components.

**Phase 2: Design System & Core UI (parallelizable)**
Building the reusable UI components like GlassPanel, TypewriterText, StatGauge, XPBar, WarpTransition, and AudioManager that the rest of the app depends on.

**Phase 3: Game State & Data Layer (parallelizable)**
Creating the game state management with save/load functionality, all 34 mission definitions, dialogue trees, and item data structures.

**Phase 4: Core Game Screens (parallelizable)**
Building the main screens: Title Screen, Character Creation, Cockpit HUD, Star Map with Canvas rendering, and the navigation bar.

**Phase 5: Game Systems (parallelizable)**
Implementing the Dialogue System, Mission Briefing/Debrief flows, Inventory, and Crew management pages.

**Phase 6: Mini-Games (parallelizable)**
Creating the six mini-games: Prompt Duel, Architect drag-and-drop puzzle, Connect wiring puzzle, Debug spot-the-bug, Command assignment, and Dialogue quiz.

**Phase 7: Planet Content (highly parallelizable — each planet is independent)**
Building out the planet-specific missions, starting with Vibe World and Debt Belt.

Continuing through the remaining planets: MCP Station, Agent Academy, Framework Nebula, Orchestration Citadel, Security Fortress, and Production Worlds, each with their own mission counts.

**Phase 8: Academy (parallelizable — each section independent)**
Developing the 10 Academy sections.

**Phase 9: Polish (parallelizable)**
Adding audio, page transitions, responsive design, and performance optimization.

**Phase 10: Deploy**
Setting up Vercel and configuring the domain.

Since this is a game with mostly UI and no traditional backend logic, I should shift away from unit testing and focus on build verification and visual checks instead — the "tests" here are really about ensuring everything renders and functions correctly.

For the testable parts, I can focus on game state logic like save/load and progression, while data definitions and UI components rely more on browser verification and interaction testing for the mini-games.

With about a week to ship and the user wanting speed through agent teams, I need to maximize parallelism across tasks. I'm also thinking about the file naming for the plan document — something like `docs/plans/2026-03-07-implementation-plan.md` makes sense.

Now I'm structuring a comprehensive but focused plan that accounts for the project's scope and the need for parallel execution. I need to finalize the tech stack details — Next.js 15 specifically with Tailwind v4 using CSS imports rather than config files, plus Motion instead of Framer Motion. Rather than query for setup commands now, I'll let the executing agents handle that with context7 when they implement. The real challenge here is that this is fundamentally a content-heavy project where the actual game framework is maybe 30% of the work, with the bulk being mission dialogues, Academy articles, and mini-game variations across 8 planets and 34 missions.

content.text:
### Animate Component Exit with `AnimatePresence` (React)

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-layout-animations

Use the `AnimatePresence` component to keep components in the DOM until their exit animations are complete, allowing elements to animate back to their origin. This is crucial for shared layout animations where an element needs to disappear gracefully.

```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {isOpen && <motion.div layoutId="modal" />}
</AnimatePresence>
```

--------------------------------

### AnimatePresence Modes: Sync, Wait, and PopLayout

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animate-presence

AnimatePresence offers different modes for handling entering and exiting children. 'sync' animates immediately, 'wait' sequences animations sequentially, and 'popLayout' removes elements from layout flow for immediate reflow.

```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="wait">
  {/* Content that animates sequentially */}
</AnimatePresence>
```

```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">
  {items.map(item => (
    <motion.li layout exit={{ opacity: 0 }} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```

--------------------------------

### AnimatePresence Component

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animate-presence

AnimatePresence is a component that allows you to animate components when they are removed from the DOM.

```APIDOC
## AnimatePresence Component

### Description
AnimatePresence is a component that allows you to animate components when they are removed from the DOM. It provides control over exit animations and layout transitions.

### Props

#### `initial` (boolean)
- **Description**: If set to `false`, `AnimatePresence` will disable any initial animations on children that are present when the component is first rendered.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence initial={false}>
  <Slide key={activeItem.id} />
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### `custom` (any)
- **Description**: Allows passing dynamic data to exit animations. This data can be accessed by children via `usePresenceData` and used to change the `exit` animation based on dynamic variants.
- **Example**:
```jsx
const variants = {
  hidden: (direction) => ({
    opacity: 0,
    x: direction === 1 ? -300 : 300
  }),
  visible: { opacity: 1, x: 0 }
}

export const Slideshow = ({ image, direction }) => (
  <AnimatePresence custom={direction}>
    <motion.img
      key={image.src}
      src={image.src}
      variants={variants}
      initial="hidden"
      animate="visible"
      exit="hidden"
    />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```

#### `mode` (string)
- **Description**: Decides how `AnimatePresence` handles entering and exiting children. Can be one of: `"sync"`, `"wait"`, or `"popLayout"`.
  - **`"sync"` (Default)**: Elements animate in and out as soon as they're added/removed. No opinion on sequencing animations or layout.
  - **`"wait"`**: The entering element will wait until the exiting child has animated out, before it animates in. Supports only one child at a time. Great for sequential animations.
  - **`"popLayout"`**: Exiting elements will be "popped" out of the page layout, allowing surrounding elements to immediately reflow. Pairs well with the `layout` prop.
- **Example for `popLayout`**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">
  {items.map(item => (
    <motion.li layout exit={{ opacity: 0 }} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- **Note for `popLayout`**: If using `popLayout` mode with custom components as immediate children, they **must** be wrapped in `React.forwardRef`.

#### `onExitComplete` (function)
- **Description**: Fires when all exiting nodes have completed animating out.

#### `propagate` (boolean)
- **Description**: If set to `true`, exit animations on children will also trigger when this `AnimatePresence` exits from a parent `AnimatePresence`. Defaults to `false`.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {show ? (
    <motion.section exit={{ opacity: 0 }}>
      <AnimatePresence propagate>
        {/* This exit prop will now fire when show is false */}
        <motion.div exit={{ x: -100 }} />
      </AnimatePresence>
    </motion.section>
  ) : null}
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### `root` (Element | ShadowRoot)
- **Description**: Root element for injecting `popLayout` styles. Defaults to `document.head` but can be set to another `ShadowRoot` for use within shadow DOM.

### Troubleshooting

#### Exit animations aren't working
- Ensure all **immediate** children get a unique `key` prop that **remains the same for that component every render**.
- **Bad Key Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {items.map((item, index) => (
    <Component key={index} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- **Preferred Key Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {items.map((item) => (
    <Component key={item.id} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- Make sure `AnimatePresence` is **outside** of the code that unmounts the element. If `AnimatePresence` itself unmounts, it can't control exit animations.
- **Incorrect Placement Example**:
```jsx
isVisible && (
  <AnimatePresence>
    <Component />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```
- **Correct Placement Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {isVisible && <Component />}
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### Layout animations not working with `mode="sync"`
- When mixing exit and layout animations, it might be necessary to wrap the group in `LayoutGroup` to ensure that components outside of `AnimatePresence` know when to perform a layout animation.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<LayoutGroup>
  <motion.ul layout>
    <AnimatePresence>
      {items.map(item => (
        <motion.li layout key={item.id} />
      ))}
    </AnimatePresence>
  </motion.ul>
</LayoutGroup>
```
```

--------------------------------

### Implement Exit Animations with AnimatePresence

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animation

Shows how to animate elements as they are removed from the DOM using `AnimatePresence` and the `exit` prop. This component keeps elements in the DOM temporarily to allow exit animations to complete.

```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {isVisible && (
    <motion.div
      key="modal"
      initial={{ opacity: 0 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1 }}
      exit={{ opacity: 0 }}
    />
  )}
</AnimatePresence>
```

--------------------------------

### AnimatePresence for Slideshows with Key Changes

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animate-presence

A practical example of using AnimatePresence with changing keys to create a slideshow effect. Each image has a unique key, allowing AnimatePresence to animate the transition between images smoothly using `initial`, `animate`, and `exit` props.

```javascript
export const Slideshow = ({ image }) => (
  <AnimatePresence>
    <motion.img
      key={image.src}
      src={image.src}
      initial={{ x: 300, opacity: 0 }}
      animate={{ x: 0, opacity: 1 }}
      exit={{ x: -300, opacity: 0 }}
    />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```

AnimatePresence offers different modes for handling entering and exiting children. 'sync' animates immediately, 'wait' sequences animations sequentially, and 'popLayout' removes elements from layout flow for immediate reflow.

```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="wait">
  {/* Content that animates sequentially */}
</AnimatePresence>
```

```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">
  {items.map(item => (
    <motion.li layout exit={{ opacity: 0 }} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```

--------------------------------

### AnimatePresence Component

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animate-presence

AnimatePresence is a component that allows you to animate components when they are removed from the DOM.

```APIDOC
## AnimatePresence Component

### Description
AnimatePresence is a component that allows you to animate components when they are removed from the DOM. It provides control over exit animations and layout transitions.

### Props

#### `initial` (boolean)
- **Description**: If set to `false`, `AnimatePresence` will disable any initial animations on children that are present when the component is first rendered.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence initial={false}>
  <Slide key={activeItem.id} />
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### `custom` (any)
- **Description**: Allows passing dynamic data to exit animations. This data can be accessed by children via `usePresenceData` and used to change the `exit` animation based on dynamic variants.
- **Example**:
```jsx
const variants = {
  hidden: (direction) => ({
    opacity: 0,
    x: direction === 1 ? -300 : 300
  }),
  visible: { opacity: 1, x: 0 }
}

export const Slideshow = ({ image, direction }) => (
  <AnimatePresence custom={direction}>
    <motion.img
      key={image.src}
      src={image.src}
      variants={variants}
      initial="hidden"
      animate="visible"
      exit="hidden"
    />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```

#### `mode` (string)
- **Description**: Decides how `AnimatePresence` handles entering and exiting children. Can be one of: `"sync"`, `"wait"`, or `"popLayout"`.
  - **`"sync"` (Default)**: Elements animate in and out as soon as they're added/removed. No opinion on sequencing animations or layout.
  - **`"wait"`**: The entering element will wait until the exiting child has animated out, before it animates in. Supports only one child at a time. Great for sequential animations.
  - **`"popLayout"`**: Exiting elements will be "popped" out of the page layout, allowing surrounding elements to immediately reflow. Pairs well with the `layout` prop.
- **Example for `popLayout`**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence mode="popLayout">
  {items.map(item => (
    <motion.li layout exit={{ opacity: 0 }} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- **Note for `popLayout`**: If using `popLayout` mode with custom components as immediate children, they **must** be wrapped in `React.forwardRef`.

#### `onExitComplete` (function)
- **Description**: Fires when all exiting nodes have completed animating out.

#### `propagate` (boolean)
- **Description**: If set to `true`, exit animations on children will also trigger when this `AnimatePresence` exits from a parent `AnimatePresence`. Defaults to `false`.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {show ? (
    <motion.section exit={{ opacity: 0 }}>
      <AnimatePresence propagate>
        {/* This exit prop will now fire when show is false */}
        <motion.div exit={{ x: -100 }} />
      </AnimatePresence>
    </motion.section>
  ) : null}
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### `root` (Element | ShadowRoot)
- **Description**: Root element for injecting `popLayout` styles. Defaults to `document.head` but can be set to another `ShadowRoot` for use within shadow DOM.

### Troubleshooting

#### Exit animations aren't working
- Ensure all **immediate** children get a unique `key` prop that **remains the same for that component every render**.
- **Bad Key Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {items.map((item, index) => (
    <Component key={index} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- **Preferred Key Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {items.map((item) => (
    <Component key={item.id} />
  ))}
</AnimatePresence>
```
- Make sure `AnimatePresence` is **outside** of the code that unmounts the element. If `AnimatePresence` itself unmounts, it can't control exit animations.
- **Incorrect Placement Example**:
```jsx
isVisible && (
  <AnimatePresence>
    <Component />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```
- **Correct Placement Example**:
```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {isVisible && <Component />}
</AnimatePresence>
```

#### Layout animations not working with `mode="sync"`
- When mixing exit and layout animations, it might be necessary to wrap the group in `LayoutGroup` to ensure that components outside of `AnimatePresence` know when to perform a layout animation.
- **Example**:
```jsx
<LayoutGroup>
  <motion.ul layout>
    <AnimatePresence>
      {items.map(item => (
        <motion.li layout key={item.id} />
      ))}
    </AnimatePresence>
  </motion.ul>
</LayoutGroup>
```
```

--------------------------------

### Implement Exit Animations with AnimatePresence

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animation

Shows how to animate elements as they are removed from the DOM using `AnimatePresence` and the `exit` prop. This component keeps elements in the DOM temporarily to allow exit animations to complete.

```jsx
<AnimatePresence>
  {isVisible && (
    <motion.div
      key="modal"
      initial={{ opacity: 0 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1 }}
      exit={{ opacity: 0 }}
    />
  )}
</AnimatePresence>
```

--------------------------------

### AnimatePresence for Slideshows with Key Changes

Source: https://motion.dev/docs/react/-animate-presence

A practical example of using AnimatePresence with changing keys to create a slideshow effect. Each image has a unique key, allowing AnimatePresence to animate the transition between images smoothly using `initial`, `animate`, and `exit` props.

```javascript
export const Slideshow = ({ image }) => (
  <AnimatePresence>
    <motion.img
      key={image.src}
      src={image.src}
      initial={{ x: 300, opacity: 0 }}
      animate={{ x: 0, opacity: 1 }}
      exit={{ x: -300, opacity: 0 }}
    />
  </AnimatePresence>
)
```

**Goal:** Build a complete interactive space exploration game that teaches vibe coding, agentic AI, and modern software engineering — from beginner to agentic developer.

**Architecture:** Next.js 15 App Router with client-side game state in localStorage. No backend. All game content defined as TypeScript data structures. Canvas-based star map. Motion for animations. Howler.js for audio. Glassmorphism UI throughout.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Motion (from `motion/react`), HTML5 Canvas, Howler.js, localStorage, Vercel

**Parallelization:** Tasks within each phase are independent and SHOULD be dispatched to parallel agents. Dependencies between phases are noted. Each task produces a working, committable unit.

**Critical Rules:**
- Import Motion from `motion/react`, NEVER from `framer-motion`
- Tailwind v4: use `@import "tailwindcss"` + `@theme` in CSS, NOT `tailwind.config.js`
